passages.t: ‘He wraps Himself in light as with a garment’
passages.happening:
Psalm 104 has no heading. It begins with the same words that opened and closed Psalm 103: “Bless the LORD, O my soul! O LORD my God, You are very great; You are clothed with splendor and majesty” (verse 1).

Then it paints God at work making the world. “He wraps Himself in light as with a garment; He stretches out the heavens like a tent” (verse 2). He makes the clouds his chariot and rides “on the wings of the wind” (verse 3). Winds and fire are his servants (verse 4).

“He set the earth on its foundations, never to be moved” (verse 5). Once deep water covered it, even the mountains (verse 6). “At Your rebuke the waters fled; at the sound of Your thunder they hurried away” (verse 7). The mountains rose and the valleys sank to their places (verse 8). “You set a boundary they cannot cross, that they may never again cover the earth” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The psalm pictures the world the way people in ancient Israel saw it. The sky is like a tent stretched over the earth. Above it are waters, and God's rooms are built on them. The earth stands on foundations. These are a poet's pictures, and the first hearers would enjoy them as pictures, much as we say the sun ‘rises’.

Israel's neighbours told stories of gods who fought the sea, as the note on Psalm 74 explains. Here there is no fight. God speaks a rebuke, and the waters simply run.

The deep waters over the earth (verse 6) remind many readers of the start of Genesis, where “darkness was over the surface of the deep” (Genesis 1:2), and God gathered the waters so dry land appeared. Others hear the flood in Noah's day, because verse 9 says the waters will ‘never again’ cover the earth, much as God promised Noah (Genesis 9:11). The psalm may be using the language of both.

Psalm 104 sings that God made the world and keeps it. It does not say how long that took or by what steps. Christians hold different views on the age of the earth and on evolution, and Psalm 104 does not take a side.
passages.later:
God answers Job with the same picture of the sea held back: “here your proud waves must stop” (Job 38:11).

John says of the Word, who became flesh in Jesus, “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3). Paul writes, “He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (Colossians 1:17).
passages.asks:
When did you last stop and look at the sky, a storm, or the line where the sea meets the land? Psalm 104 sees God's hand in all of it.

Start your praise where this psalm starts: ‘O LORD my God, You are very great.’ Then let the world around you give you reasons.

passages.t: ‘Wine that gladdens the heart of man’: a world God keeps feeding
passages.happening:
Now the psalm walks through the land. God sends springs into the valleys, and every wild animal drinks (verses 10 to 11). Birds nest by the streams and sing in the branches (verse 12). Rain falls on the mountains (verse 13).

“He makes the grass grow for the livestock and provides crops for man to cultivate, bringing forth food from the earth” (verse 14). Food for people comes in three gifts: “wine that gladdens the heart of man, oil that makes his face to shine, and bread that sustains his heart” (verse 15).

The tall trees have all they need, and storks nest in them (verses 16 to 17). Wild goats live on high mountains and rock badgers in the cliffs (verse 18).

God set the moon to mark the seasons and the sun to set (verse 19). At night the young lions hunt, and “seek their food from God” (verse 21). In the morning they go back to their dens, and “Man goes forth to his work and to his labor until evening” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The details are those of the land of Israel and its neighbours. In a land without great rivers, springs and mountain rain meant the difference between life and death. Wine, olive oil and bread were the three great crops of the land. The cedars of Lebanon were famous across the ancient world.

Notice how wide God's care is. The wild donkey, the stork, the wild goat and the lion are fed, not only farm animals and people. Many of them are of no use to anyone. God cares for them anyway. And the lions' roar is described as asking God for food.

The psalm also has a gentle rhythm of work and rest. Animals hunt at night; people work by day. Each creature has its time and place.

Scholars often compare Psalm 104 with the Great Hymn to the Aten, an Egyptian hymn from the days of Pharaoh Akhenaten, which praises the sun for bringing day after a dangerous night, sending people to work and caring for animals. Some parts of the order are alike, especially from verse 20 on. Scholars differ on what that means. Some think Israel's poets knew a form of the Egyptian hymn. Others think both drew on a common way of praising a creator, and that direct borrowing is unlikely. Either way, Psalm 104 does not praise the sun. It says God made the sun, and the sun ‘knows when to set’.
passages.later:
Jesus pointed to the same care. Of the birds he said, “They do not sow or reap or gather into barns”, yet “your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not much more valuable than they?” (Matthew 6:26).

Paul told a crowd in Lystra that God “gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17). In Genesis, God placed the first man in the garden “to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15).
passages.hard: Does this psalm tell us how to vote or which policies to support on the environment? No. It does something deeper. It shows that the world belongs to God and that he cares for every creature in it, even the ones no person needs. Christians draw from that a duty to care for the earth and its creatures, as stewards of what is God's, not ours. How to do that wisely in a given place and time is left to conscience and good judgment.
passages.asks:
Psalm 104 thanks God for wine, oil and bread: joy, health and food. What are the ordinary gifts on your table today? Thank him for them by name.

And look at the creatures you share the world with. The psalm says God feeds them. How do you treat the part of his world that is in your care?

passages.t: ‘How many are Your works’, and the first ‘Hallelujah’
passages.happening:
The singer can only marvel. “How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all; the earth is full of Your creatures” (verse 24).

He looks at the sea, full of creatures great and small (verse 25). “There the ships pass, and Leviathan, which You formed to frolic there” (verse 26).

Then he says that every creature depends on God, moment by moment. “All creatures look to You to give them their food in due season” (verse 27). And “when You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good things” (verse 28). But “when You take away their breath, they die and return to dust” (verse 29). “When You send Your Spirit, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth” (verse 30).

He prays that God would rejoice in what he has made (verse 31), and promises, “I will sing to the LORD all my life” (verse 33). He prays that sinners would vanish from the earth (verse 35). And he ends, “Bless the LORD, O my soul. Hallelujah” (verse 35).
passages.hearers:
Leviathan, the sea monster that frightened other nations, appears here as a creature God made for play. ‘You formed to frolic there’ means God made it to play. In other places Leviathan is a picture of chaos (see the note on Psalm 74). In Psalm 104 it is just one more creature, splashing in the sea God made.

Verses 29 and 30 use one Hebrew word, ruach, which can mean breath, wind or spirit. When God takes away their breath, creatures die. When he sends his Spirit, they are made. Life itself is God's gift, given breath by breath.

‘Hallelujah’ means ‘praise the LORD’. In the Psalms it first appears here, at the very end of Psalm 104. From now on it will be heard more and more, until it frames the last five psalms of the book.
passages.later:
In Genesis, God “breathed the breath of life” into the first man (Genesis 2:7). Paul tells the people of Athens that God “gives everyone life and breath and everything else” (Acts 17:25).

Paul also says that God's “invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship” (Romans 1:20). And Genesis ends its account of creation with God's verdict: “indeed, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31).
passages.hard: Why does a joyful song about creation end with a prayer that sinners vanish (verse 35)? Because in a world this good, evil is the one thing that spoils it. The prayer is for evil to be removed from God's world, and it is prayed to God, not carried out by the singer. Readers take it as a prayer that sin itself would end, or as a prayer for God's judgment on evil that refuses to turn. The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out the wider question.
passages.asks:
Every breath you take, Psalm 104 says, is from God. Take one slow breath now and thank him for it.

Then join the singer's promise: ‘I will sing to the LORD all my life.’ Not only when life is easy. All of it. The psalm has shown you enough reasons to begin.
